speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: asked the Acting Minister for Transport whether the Ministry would consider lowering the speed limit for bicycles on shared paths from the current 25 km/h for the safety of other path users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: Cyclists should slow down and give way to pedestrians, especially when approaching crowded places.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng) (for the Acting Minister for Transport)
text: The Land Transport Authority (LTA) will continue to ensure path safety and conduct education campaigns and community engagement programmes regularly to promote gracious path sharing and safe behaviour.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Speaker, I have two supplementary questions for the Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: To put things into perspective, 25 kilometres per hour would be about seven metres per second, and about 14 to 15 seconds for every 100 metres.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: That is roughly the speed of a very fit and casual jogger, somewhat like Mr Speaker, when you are running at full throttle.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: So, imagine that, Mr Speaker, the momentum of a bicycle.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And this is what pedestrians, especially the elderly staying in Mountbatten and perhaps in other areas of Singapore, are facing right now.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: So, in light of this, I will ask this question.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Would the Minister of State not consider bicycles at that speed on a path shared by the elderly, young children and adults walking their pets, to be reckless as well?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Should we not consider lowering the speed as a deterrent measure, as opposed to enforcement and education, especially when a lower speed limit will improve reaction time and safety?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: But I would like to explain that this speed limit of 25 kilometres an hour was derived by the Active Mobility Advisory Panel after extensive consultations with different users of our paths.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, the 25 kilometres an hour is for shared paths, which tend to be wider and allows for pedestrians or slow-moving users to keep to one side, which means to the left of the path, to allow for faster-moving device users to overtake them.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, if the users adhere to this code of conduct, we do allow the different users travelling at different speeds to co-exist harmoniously and safely.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And on these paths, devices which are motorised cannot be used.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: That means, only manual bicycles could be used, as well as for users of personal mobility aids.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do agree with the views expressed by the hon Ms Gho.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am respectfully of the view that I think 25 kilometres per hour, aside from those on road bikes, would be more appropriate for bicycle speed on the road rather than on a shared path.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I think most bicycles, other than road bikes, do not travel as much as that speed on shared paths or even on the roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Recently, the Minister of State mentioned that riders could, where necessary, overtake pedestrians on a shared lane by riding into the pedestrian-only lanes – if I hear him correctly from the last Sitting.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am concerned that this may be dangerous, especially riding at a higher speed of say, 20 to 25 kilometres per hour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, may I ask Minister of State, how extensive are the current public education efforts being carried on the ground, that is, on the shared paths, especially the popular shared paths, to regulate use of all users of shared paths, including advising them to lower their speed, and can these ground outreach efforts be further enhanced?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We reach out to community groups, schools, and this is important because we want users to develop good habits from young.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, yes, we will continue to reach out to as many groups as possible and targeting areas where there has been a lot of feedback or more observed higher speeds of cycling in those areas.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: We could work with grassroots, with resident groups, communities to do the outreach.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I would also like to emphasise that the speed limit is the maximum speed allowed.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: It is not the speed at which device users and cyclists should expect to sustain for any distances.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, when the path is crowded, there are obstacles in front, a slower-moving device or user in front, they should slow down and give way to them.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And if there are cases where riders or cyclists had been reckless, they will be taken to task.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: I will just make a clarification to Mr Dennis Tan's supplementary question.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: When I said earlier, at a previous Sitting about allowing device users to overtake, these are for cases where there is a pedestrian-only path beside a cycling path.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: There is no pedestrian-only path beside a shared path.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Just wanted to explain the difference in the way we design our infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, cyclist speed may not be the only factor of danger, but also the ability of these cyclists to navigate these obstacles.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My supplementary question is whether the Ministry will consider cycling pathways to be designed to co-exist on the road, especially in areas with high density of pedestrians or vulnerable individuals, like schools or silver zones.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: Having said that, cyclists and device users can cycle on and can ride on the roads.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And so, our approach has been building cycling infrastructure off roads.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: And when it is even more limited, it will be just footpaths, and on footpaths, there are restrictions on what kind of devices could be used on those.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng
text: So, in order to allow for different users of our spaces to co-exist safely and harmoniously, we really need to build a culture of sharing, of gracious use of these spaces, and for everybody to understand the rules and abide by the rules.
